chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hareez, from Ubayd ibn Zurara, who said:

I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'There is no servant who withholds a dirham from its rightful (spending) except that he will spend two in other than its rightful place; and there is no man who withholds a right from his wealth except that God Mighty and Majestic will collar him with a snake of fire on the Day of Resurrection.'

key_terms.حَقِّهِ: Its right/its due — referring to the religiously mandated channel for spending (e.g., zakat, charity)
key_terms.حَيَّةً مِنْ نَارٍ: A snake of fire — the form taken by withheld wealth as punishment on the Day of Resurrection
key_terms.طَوَّقَهُ: To collar, to put a yoke/necklace around — an eschatological punishment imagery from the Quran
key_terms.عَزَّ وَ جَلَّ: Mighty and Majestic — a standard honorific formula for God
key_terms.يَمْنَعُ: To withhold, prevent from its due place — here meaning the withholding of zakat or other obligatory financial duties

ai.seo_question: What happens to someone who withholds zakat according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) warns that withholding wealth from its obligatory duties — such as zakat — is spiritually self-defeating: the one who withholds one dirham will inevitably spend two in impermissible ways. The second clause invokes a powerful eschatological image from Quran 3:180, where those who withhold obligatory charity will have the wealth they hoarded fashioned into a collar of fire around their necks on the Day of Resurrection. This teaching was directed at Shia communities in the mid-8th century CE, for whom zakat and financial obligations were matters of active jurisprudential concern.
